utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. May the case be called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And your appearances with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: It's Morton Bergsmo and my co-counsel Nick Koumjian, and case manager Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's today start immediately with our new witness of today. Am I right, witness in open session but protected, voice distortion and face distortion?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I had understood face distortion and pseudonym only.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes. Face distortion and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, but I had asked what about voice distortion, therefore the problem with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: I apologise. There was a problem with my hearing here, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So only voice -- or only face.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Only face and pseudonym, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Pseudonym. Witness D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. And we call witness "Witness D." And the witness can be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand? First of all, my apologies that I have to address you as "Witness D" only, but it's in your interest. It's for your protection. Please understand. Could the declaration be taken from the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The OTP may start the examination-in-chief, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Initially, we would like to ask some questions to establish the identity of the witness, and we would ask that we go into private session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any objection. Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Witness, if when you give your answers to the following questions, there is a need to disclose information which could lead to your identification, you may indicate that, so that we could go into private session again. What were the working relations like in the Executive Board between the SDA and SDS members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness, slow down, so that the interpreters can hear you. Could you please repeat the answer, because we don't have it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So for me, the Executive Board is an operative body, and that is how I saw it when I started working there, as an operative non-political body. And all the positions in it were held by people who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were specialised in a particular field so that, for instance, economists who were in charge of fiscal affairs and development, then engineers, civil engineers or architects, again, in the appropriate secretariat; lawyers held posts related to law. So that at the beginning, in my view, there were no problems or disagreements in our mutual relationships and the coordination of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did the working relations change over time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: This is what happened: Direct relationships between members of the board, personal relations, did not change so much as did the method of work of the Executive Board which later blocked its activities, because the SDS towards the end started giving instructions to their members simply not to attend meetings of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: And did the SDS members of the Executive Board then attend meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As I said, at first, for quite a long time, the work was normal. Later on, if an order comes for them not to attend, they didn't attend. And then a meeting could not be held, no valid decisions could be made if they were not represented. Because half of the voting members were from the SDS and half from the SDA so that no valid decisions could be taken without the participation of both.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did the SDS members of the Executive Board seem to operate on the basis of some plan, or was there a pattern in their conduct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Whether there was a plan on their part, I really can't say. But this blockade took place later. This blockade was more reflected upon the work of the Assembly, much more than on the work of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Approximately when did this blockade start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the blockade was first in the Assembly. First it was partial, and then it was total. The first difficulties arose when the parties could not agree on certain appointments. Then later on, these obstructions occurred more and more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did the SDS members of the Executive Board want Prijedor municipality to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Certainly that was the aim. It was quite clear. They were simply, if not directly, then indirectly, dissatisfied that they were unable to implement their policies in a legal manner, through voting. They didn't -- they wanted to have this decision made for Prijedor to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina. They couldn't achieve it at the Assembly or the Executive Board through legal means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: So it was your impression at the time that this was the general SDS position in Prijedor, that Prijedor municipality should join the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. That was quite clear from other things, too. In various ways, for instance, through the media, the Kozarski Vjesnik published on the first page one day a map of the division of the town of Prijedor. Kozarski Vjesnik was closely linked to the SDS, and this was an intimation of something that they intended to achieve. They simply wanted separate Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Are you aware if the SDS or Serbian political leaders in Prijedor attempted to have a change made in the uniform of the Prijedor police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There was this tendency - I don't know whether it was an order, because I wasn't directly involved in the coordination of the SDS - but I know that this was already done in Banja Luka and in towns in which they had an undisputed majority, so they were able to outvote smaller parties and peoples like Bosanska Dubica and Bosanski Novi where they had already introduced new uniforms. And I know that the chief of police from Banja Luka came to the Prijedor police to have talks in this connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Who was that who came from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I wasn't present at that meeting, but I heard about it, and that it was Stojan Zupljanin and there were some other leaders from Prijedor, according to what I heard. As I said, I wasn't there. The chief of police, members of the police, I don't know whether it was the president of the municipality, the presidents of the SDS and SDA parties, I think both of them were there. Who else was there, I don't know. This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What is your source for this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I heard this in very brief form from the chief of police at the time in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did he tell you more about this meeting that occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He spoke very briefly about it. He said that the atmosphere was tense because it could be felt that the Serb policemen had already received certain instructions, but were waiting for some sort of a signal, that he wasn't in favour of this, and that no concrete agreement had been reached. That is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Could you give the name of the chief of police at the time to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What was his ethnic or religious identity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to ask a couple of questions that may require private session. I don't believe that they will take a long time to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness please give us the exact name of the chief of police, Hasan and then could you please spell the name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic. [In English] It's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's correct. Then we proceed in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor municipality report to the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, actually. The highest legislative body is the Municipal Assembly, and the Executive Board is an organ of the assembly. It's official name is "the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly" so it's a body that is subordinated to the Municipal Assembly, and it is the duty of the Executive Board to report on its work to the assembly. And also many issues were not within the terms of reference of the Executive Board. It just makes proposals, and it is the assembly that passes the law and turns these proposals into law. Afterwards, this didn't function so well because the assembly was blocked, the work of the assembly was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: In practical terms, how did the reporting from the Executive Board to the Municipal Assembly function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The Executive Board, if it held a session and there were certain issues that needed to be verified by the Assembly, then those documents would be sent to the secretary of the Municipal Assembly. Then, in cooperation with the president or vice-president, it is the duty of the secretary to prepare the agenda for the Assembly meeting including the items prepared by the Executive Board, including a report on the work of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: And could any member of the Executive Board be present in the Assembly when there was reporting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. It was a rule that if an item was on the agenda proposed by the Executive Board, then the people who had prepared the material, the documents, from the Executive Board should explain those documents before the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Was the position as president of the Municipal Assembly more important in the hierarchy than that as president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It is hard to say with precision and clarity, but let me try and explain. The Municipal Assembly, as an assembly, is a higher-level body than the Executive Board. It is the highest legislative body. And as such, the position of the Municipal Assembly and of the mayor should be the highest function, though the position of the president of the Executive Board is also quite high in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: I was planning to ask some further questions relevant to the institution on which the witness served concerning the work of that institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court what the abbreviation "SDK" stands for.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I can explain the abbreviation, of course, but I'm not an expert in economy. I couldn't give any explanation as to its work. However the acronym itself stands for “Sluzba Drustvenog Knjigovodstva”, public accountancy service. It is actually a local auditing agency, public auditing body which supervised all financial transactions and payments which are done in a given area. So all these -- transactions are done in through this particular office. It is very difficult to explain this to someone coming from the west. This system has now been abandoned in Bosnia, but it used to be an institution through which money transactions and payments were done. At least, that's how I understood the service to be. They had the overall control over financial transactions, and they were in charge of supervising the legality of such transactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Does this mean that financial transactions did not happen through banks and postal services but happened through the SDK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did the SDS in Prijedor have a position on reorganisation of the SDK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As far as the overall, local policy is concerned, I think that the SDK was a very significant institution for them because as I heard in Sanski Most and in other towns such as Bosanski Novi and Bosanska Dubica, the SDS had completely taken over the SDK. So it was very obvious that they were trying to do the same in Prijedor. An incident to that effect actually occurred, an incident I heard about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: And what was that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: From what I heard, it appears that the lady who was the acting director of the SDK in Prijedor, Mrs. Hava Bahtijaragic, I believe is her name, called the president of the municipality and she complained that she had had a very unpleasant visit by the leaders of the SDS who had threatened her telling her that she should change the way the service was working and that the Serb SDK should be established; that is, that she should also adopt the tendencies towards further regionalisation as it was the case in the area. Mico Kovacevic ^ said that the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor was also there. So apparently, there was a group of people who threatened her, who endeavoured to establish a Serb SDK in Prijedor. I think it happened in early April or late March that year if memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to show the witness a document. That is Document 87 on the Rule 65 ter exhibit list of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the provisional number would be S18.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: May I ask the witness to read the heading of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If my learned friend could tell us the ERN number so we can find the document, so we can be able to follow it as well. We probably have it, but we don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Of course. It is, for the translation -- let me give you the original first which is, since you have the benefit of command of the language, 02116450, one page only. And for the translation, 03041509 with a second page which ends with 10 instead of 09.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please wait until the Defence has the document before ... Defence, you have got another copy? Would it be possible for the OTP to provide another copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We did provide a copy this morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would be so kind as to read the headings of the document, including the indication of place and date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "Social accounting service in SR, socialist republic, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo central office, general director." Do you want me Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes, please. If you could read the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, okay. "Today, the 10th of April, 1992, representatives of the SDS of Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica and Sanski Most, and the presidents of the municipalities of Bosanska Dubica, Bosanski Novi and Sanski Most, and the chairman of the executive committee of Prijedor, Milan Kovacevic accompanied by the president of the SDS party, Milomir Stakic, visited this branch office with the request that the Serbian state take over the branch office and the field offices. "They demanded an immediate implementation of the decision which you will find enclosed in the attachment, and they also demand that Serbian SDKs be formed, that is, that the representatives of the SDS take over the leading positions in all four municipalities according to an organisational plan that they have already implemented."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: And then, if you could go down to the third-last paragraph and read that and the second-to-last paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Okay. "In Bosanski Novi, they have already installed a man as a field office director, of which I informed you yesterday, and in Bosanska Dubica the director is working together with the SDS because he travelled to Bosanska Gradiska in order to open an account. "In Sanski Most, an ethnic Serb was appointed acting director, but they, too, decided to merge with Banja Luka where they have opened accounts."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: I actually meant the next two paragraphs, if you could kindly proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. "The Prijedor SDS party is demanding the same or the possible break away of the Serbian SDK, which is what the others also want. "They state that, in their words, this separation should be done in a peaceful way in order to avoid the use of force, because as they said, they were ready for anything if by Monday there is no agreement on the above. "I ask for instructions or perhaps for your intervention."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this would be an appropriate time for break now. We resume at 11.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated, and may we proceed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Prosecution wishes to ask a question which would, again, bear on the identity of the witness. It is essentially only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then for one question and the answer, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to show the witness and to tender Document 95 on our Rule 65 ter list, Document 95. The ERN number of the original is at the bottom of the page, 0016209, and it has two pages. The translation, ERN number is at the top right corner of the English translation are 03016149 and 150, page 2. Could this document be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be provisional S19.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: May I ask the witness to slowly read the heading of the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Prijedor municipality, Executive Board, extract from the minutes of a meeting of businessmen and representatives of the Prijedor municipality held on the 21st of April, 1992, on the premises of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, the large hall, commencing at 10.20 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Could I then ask you to go down to where it says "agenda" in the English version, and read from there, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [In English] Page 2 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes, in the original that would be on page 2 where it starts Dnevni red.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "For this meeting, the following agenda was proposed and adopted: 1. Economic issues in Prijedor municipality. In the discussion on this agenda item, a large number of attending businessmen from Prijedor municipality took part, representatives of banks, the SDK, and Prijedor Municipal Assembly. "After the discussion on this agenda item, the following conclusion was adopted."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Then just read the first line after the number 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "1. A working group was appointed consisting of the following: Dzemal Sefer, director of Prijedor PBS."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think we need to read the list of names. Does this document contain a summary of minutes of the meeting you just referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. In the conclusions under point 2, you will find what I mentioned a moment ago, that this group was formed to examine the possibilities and the purpose of this proposal that was the subject of discussion. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: The Prosecution would then like to show the witness and introduce Document Number 101 on the Rule 65 ter exhibit list, that's Number 101. The ERN number of the one page original is 0038531. That is indicated in the lower half of the right side. The ERN number of the English translation is 01902874. Does the witness have a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It will be provisional S20.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Please read slowly the heading of this document, including the indicated date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "The Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serbian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. municipality of Prijedor, Executive Board, number 04/92. Date: 29th April, 1992. "At a session of the Executive Board of the Serbian Assembly of Prijedor municipality held on the 29th of April, 1992, the following decision was adopted: "1. The Prijedor branch of the SDK is hereby joined to the SDK of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina. "2. Slobodan Goronic, graduate in law, is appointed acting director of the Prijedor SDK by the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. "3. This decision takes effect on the day of its adoption." "The president of the Executive Board, Dr. Milan Kovacevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Please read the text in the stamp in the original.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Serbian assembly of Prijedor municipality. SDS." That is the stamp -- their stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Given the date of this document, 29th of April, 1992, do you have any comments on the significance of the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: That date, the 29th to the 30th, was when power was illegally taken over in Prijedor so that probably this was one in a series of preparatory acts for the illegal takeover, because for me, this is an illegal document of an illegal body because a Serbian Executive Board was an illegal organ that was never legally elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What was -- why was it so important to secure control over the SDK, in your view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I said earlier on that I am not an economic or financial expert, but I noticed a long time ago that there was a large concentration of efforts for the Serbs to take over control of the SDK, because it controlled financial transactions and payments. All payments which are then taxed, republican taxes, municipal taxes. So this share of those funds was not intended to go towards the republic Sarajevo, but rather the region. And for them, it was very important to have control over monetary transactions and payments. I understood that because after all, money is a source of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Was the region controlled by the SDS at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As far as I know, such moves had been taken earlier on in Banja Luka and the other surrounding towns that I have mentioned in which the SDA was dominant, in Dubica, Sanski Most, and so on. Because this was done in this way because there was no way of doing it legally, so the document you showed earlier on was an attempt by a legal body to legalise this move. So an illegal body had to be formed to pass an illegal document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request that we briefly go into private session again in order to protect the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What was the significance of the Council for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Council for National Defence was involved with matters regarding security in case of problems in the area of the Prijedor municipality. If there are certain operational problems. It was not a legislative body. It was a body which was part of the Municipal Assembly for the purpose carrying out some specific policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to introduce -- to show the witness and to introduce Document Number 90, 90 on the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The original language version has ERN numbers 00574584 and 85, that's indicated at the top of the document. The English translation has ERN number 01107402 and 03, also indicated at the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisionally S21.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: May I ask the witness to read the document from the top, and not to do so too fast.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Very well. "09.59." It probably indicates the time. "45100, SO BL YU". If I can read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What would that stand for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Could it stand for Municipal Assembly, Skupstina [phoen] Opstina, Banja Luka, Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I simply don't know. I cannot recognise the postal code. As far as I remember, the Banja Luka postal code was 78. I see the abbreviation BL, however, I don't recognise the number. I don't know what 45100 stands for. I cannot explain this because I was not familiar with the document. There follows another number which I cannot explain, "41505 SOP LE YU." Whether this is a telefax system sign, I don't know. "Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of National Defence, Sarajevo. Number 1/92. Date: 16th of April, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: You may continue down to the first decision.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "To the governments of the AR, I believe, Autonomous Region, and the SAO, of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to all municipalities: Pursuant to Article 68 and in accordance with Article 81 of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of BH, SBiH, at its session held on the 15th of April, 1992, the Presidency of SBiH adopted the following decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Please read the first decision.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "1. The Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be established as an armed force of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Command and control Territorial Defence will be exercised: municipal, district, and regional staffs, and the republican of the SBih TO."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Could you then read from where it says "explanation" "obrazlozenje".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "Explanation: 1. Those municipal TO staffs which have until now functioned well shall remain in their existing formation and composition. Establish TO staffs in newly established Serbian municipalities along the same line. "Two --"

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at the time have any information about the existence of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, I really didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What is the significance of this document as far as you can see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Whenever I see a document for the first time -- well, it's difficult to comment. But what I can tell you is that it seems to me that it is an attempt to establish a newly ethnic army on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They talk about a Serb force here, so it would have been a parallel armed force, apart from the official forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Second, I think that this document was issued by a body which was not part of the official institutions of the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: When it says in explanation one: "Establish TO staffs in newly established Serbian municipalities along the same lines," what do you think that would refer to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I think that the following is clear in this document: As I have already indicated, in those municipalities where the SDS had clear majority, there were no problems. They had already implemented their objectives. However, in the municipalities where they were unable to achieve their goals through legal means, that is, to establish a one-nation state, they divided these municipalities and set up Serb portions of these municipalities, or they took over power in these municipalities and established them as Serb municipalities. So this is how I understand it. This is what they mean by "newly established Serbian municipalities".

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: And you obtained no information at the time, in the second half of April of 1992, about such developments in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, not at all. If I may add a further comment, from this I can conclude that they had a very well-organised system of information which was not part of the official institutions. So official institutions did not have any insight into this, but I'm sure that they must have had very good cooperation at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain to the Trial Chamber the significance of a "TO staff"? What does it stand for and what is its significance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence, as its name indicates, is an organisation designed to defend a specific territory. It was not an army; it was not a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. military at the level of a state, which was supposed to function at the level of the state with its military units. These were regional units which in cases of mobilisation are activated and used for the purposes of defence in a given territory. That is how I understand the meaning of the term "the Territorial Defence." So these staffs were locally established and had jurisdiction over certain territories, specific territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: If you look again at the text in the second section called "Odluku," "decision," would you please read the first section there. This is not the first section called "decision" but the second section called "decision."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "Decision, 1. A state of an imminent threat of war is hereby declared. 2." --

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have information at the time that a Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had declared an imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: If I can, just for the record, go to the very end of the document, after the name of the Serbian national defence minister, Bogdan Subotic, there are two text lines. Could you briefly read those two lines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "Transmitted by Vukovic on the 16th of April, 1992 at 10 hours 6 minutes. Received for Banja Luka Jerko Batinar." Then there's a plus and a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, to move on, ever hear about the existence of parallel Serbian government structures prior to the takeover of power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They even broadcast it over the Prijedor radio. I didn't hear it directly, but it was confirmed later on. One day, they just announced that they had established their government, that is, the Executive Board and the head of the police and a number of other officials. They mentioned the name of the president of the executive council and some other names. I didn't hear it directly, as I said, but I learned that they had appointed their representatives, Serb representatives, to the official positions in Prijedor. When this was announced, I know that the president of the municipality, Mr. Cehajic, whom we met at the Kozara Putevi Company, and Kovacevic was there as well, so he asked him what it meant. How come it was now announced over the radio that Serbs had proclaimed their government? And he said - he was very specific - he said it was just a political move by the SDS. So in other words, he actually confirmed what happened, although he didn't ascribe much significance to it by explaining that it was a mere political move. However, subsequently it turned out that they already had their men to be appointed to various positions in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Was it President Cehajic who informed you of what had been announced in the media about such parallel structures as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Court what happened during the takeover at the end of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Obviously, I didn't expect anything of the kind to happen. I was getting ready to go to work, and the phone rang. It was still quite early. And it was the chief of police, Mr. Talundzic who called me, and he said: "Are you getting ready to go to work?" I said "Yes." "There is no need for you to go to work." He said. "Tusic, myself and others had been to the municipality, and it seems that they are returning all SDA people and sending them home. If you look out through the window, you will see people in uniform." And it was true. I looked out of my window, and I realised that there were a lot of people in uniform with weapons all around the town. And he also told me that their guards had been positioned at various locations around the town, at the mine, in front of the banks, the SDK. This is what he saw on the way home. So I stayed home that day. I didn't go out. It was a shock, I must say, and I -- everyone could see that it was an illegal military Putsch, and that the takeover of power had been carried out illegally and with weapons because it was perfectly clear they were armed. So my initial reaction, as I said, it was a shock. Then we had to figure out what to do. The population was upset because the way this takeover of power had been carried out. If a takeover is carried out with weapons and with threat of force, then one can expect anything. I spoke over the telephone with the people who were removed from their positions, and we tried to see what should be done. But we concluded that there was actually nothing we could do at the time but to wait and to see what would happen. As I said, there was nothing we could do. We didn't have any influence any more. So those of us who had been appointed to various positions were the first ones to be dismissed. But other dismissals soon followed in various local companies, and they, of course, targeted non-Serbs. This was all done very openly, and my wife, for example, was immediately dismissed. And other non-Serbs from other local companies, without any explanation. They were simply told that they could no longer be employed. So as I said, initially, there was just tension and confusion. But very soon, people start thinking about leaving and going to an area which would be safe, because we didn't know what would happen. It was relatively peaceful during the first days. As far as we heard later on, they were busy with positioning their people to the functions that they believed to be important. And almost all of such functions were important. So after a few very peaceful days, arrests started. As far as I know, the local leaders were arrested, such as the president of the Municipal Assembly, the legal president of the Municipal Assembly, and he was arrested and taken away. I heard about a number of people who were taken away in this manner. The president of the Court, the public attorney, a number of doctors. And then the uncertain times began, the days were getting very difficult because of the psychological pressure. We knew that people were being arrested without any justification, without any reason, without any charges having been brought against them. These charges were later on fabricated. Well, there was no need to fabricate any charges actually. But what caused an even greater psychosis were the news broadcast by Radio Prijedor and the news which were published in Kozarski Vjesnik. They spread hatred towards non-Serb population through the media. It was a kind of hatred, a very primitive hatred and primitive propaganda which was difficult to explain to anyone with even the modest education. They tried to inspire hatred towards non-Serbs as much as it was possible. When Mr. Ganic's, Ejub Ganic was mentioned for example, his last name was pronounced as "Ganici," so that it would resemble the Albanian version of the name. When the name of Mr. Medunjanin was mentioned and he was the secretary of the National Defence -- am I speaking too fast? His name was always pronounced "Medunjani," so it would resemble an Albanian surname. So this was a kind of very low propaganda in order to instill as much hatred as possible towards that population. When the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Haris Silajdzic was mentioned, he was never referred to as Minister Silajdzic but as Hodza Silajdzic, only because this gentleman spoke Arabic fluently, and so that's why he was called a hodza. So it was through this type of propaganda that the atmosphere in town changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What is a hodza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: An Islamic priest. I can say that through this propaganda and through this dissemination of fear and hatred they tried to intimidate the population as much as possible and tell them there was no place for them in the municipality. A very large mosque was destroyed at the time together with the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: And what was the impact on the non-Serbian population of this propaganda?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The impact was such that it created fear. It's difficult to describe what happened and what the atmosphere was. One day meant one year for me in those days, living in an environment of that kind. Because people were being taken away systematically, and we heard that they were being killed in the most atrocious ways in various camps, such as Omarska, for example, that they were beaten to death in a most bestial fashion. That is what we heard, that people were being killed in this way. Of course, I tried to hide, and I managed to hide. I went to live in an empty apartment at the time. But it is interesting to note what ordinary people thought at the time. I called a colleague of mine, an engineer, and I asked him whether he had a place to hide. And he said: "Why should I go into hiding? I haven't done anything wrong." And it sounded perfectly normal. However, a few days later, he disappeared. So whether one was guilty of something or not didn't matter. All that matter was that he or she was a non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: When you say "he disappeared", what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I know that he went to a camp and that he never returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Should we briefly go into private session to get the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Was there at some stage a call for supervisors to return to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: First of all, I assume -- let me say first that I hid in an apartment that happened to be empty, and I was alone there. My access to information was such that I could occasionally listen to a battery-operated radio. My impression was that, first of all, they dismissed all non-Serbs; and secondly, they couldn't reach some they wanted to reach because they had been dismissed. And in order, perhaps, to facilitate their access to them, there was a proclamation that executives, leading people should return to work to be interviewed and to hand over their duty to their successors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did you report to duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I personally saw what it was about and who we were dealing with, because I can also say that throughout my life, I worked together with people of all ethnicities. But it was during those days that the world fell apart for me. So it never even occurred to me to report anywhere. I simply had no trust in anyone any more. I do know of people who did report for duty, that they disappeared. I even had telephone contact with my wife in such a way that I wouldn't call her, but she would call me. And after the telephone would ring a certain number of times, then I would call her back. So I heard that an acquaintance of ours, who was a manager, that he reported and he hoped he would be released. So she advised me to do the same because it was difficult for me. I was alone, separated from my family. However, it never even occurred to me to do that. And that man was later killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Maybe in private session, we could have his name, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Do you know where he was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He was killed in the Omarska camp. He was killed by being beaten to death. That was the way in which he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What did you learn about the Bosnian Serb Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: What I was able to learn, or guess at, was based on my rare occasions when I listened to the radio, because I had to save on the batteries so as to be informed as to what was going on. For me, the Crisis Staff meant fear. I had the impression that everything that was being done in Prijedor, absolutely everything, that behind it stood the Crisis Staff. This applied to both the civilian and the military and paramilitary activities. People were rounded up, taken away, and killed. Talking about this, I watched with my own eyes how the old city was destroyed. And later, I heard on the radio that they said in their report, when some foreign visitors came, they showed them the old town which -- they said it had been destroyed by combat operations, and I knew it was a lie because I watched it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Were there references to the Crisis Staff on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently. Whenever anything important for the town happened, no name was mentioned, but simply "the Crisis Staff." It was a "proclamation of the Crisis Staff." In my impression, it was the highest level body, but for me it simply meant fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: You say that it was said that it was a "proclamation of the Crisis Staff." Was this a standard term that was being used on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I think it was. A "proclamation" or "announcement" or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: How did you spend your time after the takeover of power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As I have said, the first few days were relatively peaceful. However, after the arrests started, I already thought about the need to seek shelter, only I didn't know where, where to go. One night, I slept at my neighbours. However, later, I moved to another building, to an empty apartment owned by a relative who happened to be in hospital in Banja Luka at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did you stay indoors most of the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did you experience psychological pressure from the situation you were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, of course. First of all, there was uncertainty, fear for one's life and what would happen next to myself and my family. Secondly, I was separated from my family, as they were in our apartment and I was in another apartment. And because every day, one would hear that someone else had been taken away so that there was uncertainty every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did you have children at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: How old were they at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They were small children, born in 1987 and 1982, my younger daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: In terms of what you eyewitnessed during this period, did you ever see one of your neighbours or neighbours of yours being arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cehajic was arrested. And that very moment, I called up a colleague of mine to tell him that Cehajic had been arrested and that it would probably be a good idea for us to seek shelter somewhere, because we could see that people were being arrested without any charges. And then my colleague said: "Wait a minute. Somebody's calling me. Call me later." However, when I called him a couple of minutes later, his wife answered saying that the policeman had taken him away and the person who was ringing were the police, in fact, when I was calling.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to this person later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He is no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Do you know if he was killed and where he was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We heard that they were killed in Omarska. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We should go in private session for the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Who arrested Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Policemen in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did they have normal police uniforms, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, yes. They also had machine-guns on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Do you know the wife of the late President Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What was her profession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: She was a physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Was she working with President Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I knew, they were colleagues from work, and they knew each other from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did she say anything about why her husband had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I spoke to her. She went directly to see Kovacevic, because she believed or she wanted to believe him because he was a colleague of hers, and she hoped to get some assistance from him. And she was given a very strange and rather nonchalant, unclear answer, and that is that Cehajic was arrested really because they were unable to arrest the president of the SDA. So they arrested him. That answer was rather strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did the police ever come to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. First, the police would come when it was announced on the radio that apartments would be searched for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Two policemen came to my apartment, and they searched the whole apartment. And then they took my two children - you know now how old they were - separately to a separate room, and then they questioned them in detail, whether I had any weapons. And this I learned from them later about this, because I had no access there. They tried in a perfidious way to get answers from them, taking bullets out of their pockets: "Did your father have anything like this or that?" So imagine such small children should be humiliated in this way and be interrogated by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Have the children had problems or have there been manifestations of problems based on this incident later? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It's very hard to know the psychology of children. And at that particular moment, one only thinks of safety, one's own safety and the safety of the whole family. And this entire atmosphere of pressure, one necessarily feels directly, but it is only later on that one realises how this overall atmosphere and pressure and this inexplicable pressure on the non-Serb population is manifested much later. When we reached free territory, maybe after eight months of life like this, I was astonished when my younger daughter asked me: "How is it that we can speak out loud now?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage we were planning to go into another aspect of what the witness had eyewitnessed at that time. So we can break at this point, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is an appropriate time. So we adjourn now and resume at 2.00 sharp. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.18 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May we continue immediately with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Before we move on to the subject I had alluded to before we broke for lunch, allow me to ask a few additional questions concerning the search of the apartment of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: After your apartment had been searched, were other apartments in your building also searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I think that only the apartments inhabited by non-Serbs were searched because the apartments in which Serbs lived were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Through your job your --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Excuse me. During the search of the apartment, since you asked me, I forgot to mention that when they were leaving the apartment, these two policeman told my wife, actually one of them who was a reserve police officer and who knew her by sight from work, he said "You better flee and try to hide somewhere because here you not safe."

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Through your job or your position, had you been given a pistol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [redacted] were issued with a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honour, do we address the record? It seems to me that the information that was just offered preferably had been given in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to make a matter of principle now, but in principal, the hearings have to be public. It is a question of transparency and this principal of public hearing should prevail. Already this morning I am afraid sometimes I granted too much possibilities for hearing in closed session; therefore, I think the public should know what has happened and it is only for the protection of the witness we go in closed session. Therefore, I can't see a reason for this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: What happened to the pistol that you had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I returned it through an acquaintance of mine. I gave it to him and told him to take it back to the Secretary of National Defence. I returned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Was this prior to the police search of your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, this was before the search.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: So at the time of the search, you did not possess any weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did you witness any use of force from the window of the apartment in which you were staying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I can say that during my stay in this other apartment where I was alone and isolated from my family, I witnessed a lot of things. One morning I remember in particular it was a foggy day, and shooting could be heard coming from all sides. After the fog had cleared a little I saw many vehicles carrying soldiers and police officers. I saw trucks carrying dead bodies. I could see their legs or feet hanging from those trucks or other similar vehicles. And since this part of town, this neighbourhood is called Stari Grad, the old town of Prijedor, I saw a tank which had pointed its barrel towards the neighbourhood of Stari Grad and opened fire. After a while after it had stopped firing and destroying the old town, I didn't understand what was going on. I was merely observing the events from my window. After that, I saw a number of buses which were parked alongside the edge of the Stari Grad neighbourhood, and I could see people leaving Stari Grad in columns. These people were civilians, men, women and children, and boarding these buses, the buses that were parked there. After the buses had picked these people, they took them somewhere, I don't know exactly where, probably to a camp. Later on, I could see various civilian and military vehicles coming to the area. I saw people in uniform going to Stari Grad and taking away everything they could find there. I saw them taking this property and loading it onto the vehicles. The area had lot of small businesses, lot of cafes there. So I concluded that a plunder of Stari Grad had started. I remember a man in uniform standing by a vehicle who was not able to load everything that he had into the trunk, so he put many things inside the car and the car was eventually so full of things that he could hardly see out of the car. He drove with difficulty as a result of that. This took place some 100, 150 metres away from where I was. After this looting was finished, I saw a number of houses being set on fire. So a systematic destruction of the Old Town started, house by house. There was a mosque next to the building where I took shelter, some 20 or 30 metres away from this building, some people entered the mosque and set the carpets on fire, first. And I could hear through the door that the people who lived in the building where I was, I could hear that they were concerned and worried, not because of the fact that the mosque had been set on fire, but they were afraid that the fire would spread to the building. So I could observe the destruction of the houses in Stari Grad and the arson which went house by house. Later on -- later on I heard over the radio that the destruction was the result of combat activities, which was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did you see those who started the fires?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Those were people in military uniforms, camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Were all the persons who were engaged in the attack on Stari Grad in camouflage uniforms, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, in these operations, it was mostly people wearing camouflage uniforms, but there were also individuals in uniforms of the reserve police force who looted the houses. But those who carried out the destruction by throwing various explosives were mostly people wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: And the tank you refer to, was that a regular army tank type?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we just have a break for urgency of time. We are thinking your request for redaction of at 206, this redaction should be granted. Any objections? Thank you. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: With that redaction, would the affirmative answer of the witness also be redacted or only his qualifying sentence that followed? It is in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All the necessary is redacted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to a tank that you had eyewitnesses that was involved in the attack on Stari Grad. Was this a normal army tank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, it was an ordinary military tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did you see any armed persons who were engaged in combat activities against the uniformed soldiers and the other Serbian armed personnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, I did not see them. I just heard the shooting early that morning. As I said, it was a foggy morning, but once the fog had cleared up, I was able to see this tank and a column of people leaving Stari Grad. They were all civilians who eventually boarded the buses that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Please explain to the Court what Stari Grad is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As the name itself indicates, it is the old centre of the town. It is the area where the town of Prijedor began. But what is characteristic about the old town, about Stari Grad and what contributed to it being totally destructed is the fact that it was built in the old traditional Bosniak architecture, even some -- there were lots of buildings, lots of houses that were protected because of the architectural value and because of the historical importance. And one other thing which was also very important and which was a characteristic of the old town was the fact that it was all inhabited by Muslims, by Bosniaks, and it consisted of houses that were built in the typical Bosniak tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Do you know what is today where Stari Grad used to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, if I may, let me just say that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. several days after this destruction of Stari Grad, heavy machines arrived - I don't know where they had come from, probably from some construction companies - and they completed the job. They levelled the area of Stari Grad. So no one would recognise this as Stari Grad any more. As for your question, after the area was razed to the ground, of course there were no houses left, no structures standing, it was just a clearing and now with the help and the approval of the International Community, they started building the old houses, that is the houses belonged to -- which belonged to the former residents, to the survivors. I heard that several such houses had been built in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: You mentioned that it had been reported that Stari Grad was destroyed as a consequence of combat activity. As far as you know, had there been any provocation prior to the destruction of Stari Grad which you have described to the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As I have already indicated, all the information that I was able to gather being there was through the local radio, Prijedor radio. I was trying to save batteries as much as I could. So this was the type of information that I was able to receive, apart from the information given to me by my wife who went out from time to time to the market, for example. I, according to the information that I had at the time, didn't know of any such provocations. But I know that the local radio very often announced the presence of Green Berets in Kozarac, several thousand, for example, which was a very clear sign for the mobilisation of citizens. I know that this by no means was true, but whether there were minor incidents here and there I don't know that because I did not personally see them; I did not experience them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: During the period when you were in hiding, were you ever taken to the police station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the time -- actually, during my stay in this apartment, I didn't go out and since my batteries were dying, I made a mistake and went to my apartment to get the battery from the car so that I could listen to the radio again. As I entered the apartment - I believe it was at the beginning of June - so when I got into the apartment carrying this battery, I think it was in the early afternoon hours, an hour later I heard a very loud knock on the door. And when we opened the door, because we had to open the door, there were six police officers there. They said that I had been seen around town on that day wearing a military uniform. They must have -- they had to have some kind of explanation, some kind of accusation when they came for people. They searched me, first of all, in the apartment and then they searched me once again when they took me downstairs. After the search I was taken to the police station. I think I was fortunate because many of my friends or acquaintances saw that I was being taken to the station, so people thought that I was no longer there, that I disappeared. I think it was on the 11th of June. So when I got to the police station, I noticed a major commotion there, a lot of people running around and I thought that perhaps it was because of the funeral which was organised on that day, the funeral of one of their combatants, Karlica was his name, I believe. So it was my impression that this event actually helped me because they started looking for a vehicle that would take me to Omarska, but it seems that most of the police force and the vehicles were mobilised for the purposes of this funeral. So after a while, after I had waited for about 10 or 15 minutes in the corridor of the police building, I was approached by a police officer who told me, you can go home now, but you should not leave Prijedor because we will come for you again. And that is how I went back home hiding around buildings and I left and went to this other apartment again. It was then that I learned from my wife that many of my neighbours thought that I was taken to Omarska on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: How did your family survive and cope with the situation during the period when you were in hiding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: First of all, as was the case with other Bosniak or rather non-Serbs, I did not work. So we had to find some money in order to buy groceries; our supplies were running out. My wife went to the local market and sold a lot of things, a lot of our belonging from our apartment. But this was also a dangerous thing to do, especially if you wanted to sell more valuable things because we heard of cases when people tried to sell more valuable things that it cost them their lives. We heard of a man who had sold a cow because a cow was quite expensive. We heard about what happened later. The people to whom he had sold the cow later came to his house to get the money back and to kill him. So we tried to survive as best as we could, all the while looking for a solution to leave the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: How were you or your family trying to find a way to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I couldn't really participate in those efforts because I couldn't appear in public, and it was my wife who sought for a way out. There was the Red Cross, that was very dangerous to take one of their convoys, and also because we were well known in Prijedor. So she tried to find some other convoys and she found a more reliable convoy in Banja Luka. And we tried to get out through one of the organisations in Banja Luka where we were not well known. And there were professional organisations who engaged in resettlement, the resettlement of non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: We will return to how you left Prijedor shortly. You have referred to the role played by the local media that some of the announcements created fear in the population. Could you give some examples of that kind of announcement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Even the most ordinary news item referring to the humiliation of other peoples or the fear of other peoples and there was evident efforts to mobilise, galvanize the Serbs. There were reports, features for instance, about a doctor in hospital. I remember in this particular case, he was a Croat, and apparently because he badly treated Serb patients, some had died, this already was an indication that that person would not fare well. And a short while after that programme, the man was taken to a camp. So every report was permeated with hatred for other peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: You have referred to what you called "Green Berets." Were there reports about the presence or activities of Green Berets in the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I just said a moment ago that when a report appears about preparations by the Green Berets, this was already a clue that they were getting ready to attack someone. They sought an excuse, a pretext in order to legalise their crimes. That was the attitude of the media. The position was that other people were jeopardising the Serbs and they realised that to kill a non-Serb was not illegal. It was a terrible atmosphere one that is difficult and impossible to describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: When we refer to media at that time in Prijedor, was there more than one main media organ? Was there more than the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: What I was able to hear was only Radio Prijedor. Now, whether there were others, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Was there a newspaper, a local newspaper with broad circulation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Kozarski Vjesnik and journalists of that newspaper were also reporters on Radio Prijedor. In a sense, they all belonged to a single broadcasting company. They were accommodated in the same building, almost in the same premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: In your judgment, did the Crisis Staff control this broadcasting company, this group of journalists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: What kind of control there was and what kind of relationship existed between them, I can't say. But I had the feeling that they were acting in the spirit of what was happening in Prijedor and in line with the moves being made by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Are you aware of any critical report on the Crisis Staff or description of the Crisis Staff on the radio after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: When you were hiding in the apartment other than your home, did Serbian forces ever visit that apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. This was also a rather difficult situation for me. In this whole series of events, there were of course, worse. I heard loud banging on the entrance door downstairs as I was in the apartment. I rarely opened the door. I went out in the evening, sometimes, to go to my own apartment. I heard this banging on doors approaching mine. They knocked on my door. I opened. There were two men in uniform wearing camouflage uniforms with so-called red berets - what formation that was, I don't know - and they said that they were looking for weapons as they had been told that someone was shooting from this building. However, at the top of that building was Serb snipers, so that I doubt the truthfulness of what he was -- what they were saying. However, when I showed my ID card, when they saw that I was a Bosniak and that there was another name on the apartment door and not mine, the man who was superior, obviously, ordered this other one that I should be made to kneel down at the point of a gun. He put his rifle, leaned it on my head. He said that he would set the apartment on fire if he found any weapons and that he should guard me like that while he went upstairs. So I stayed there with the barrel of the gun leaning against my head. After some time, however, one could hear the opening of several doors upstairs and then a very loud noise. This was the hallway so I didn't know whether it was a shot or something else. After a period of time, this other man ran down the steps caught the other one by the shoulder and they ran out. I went inside again and closed the door in shock. I realised later what had saved me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I learned in the corridor, from neighbours who were living there, through the door that they were talking, that the second man who went upstairs from door to door, that he came across the door that he knocked on and I learnt that a man lived there who either couldn't hear well or was sick or who just didn't react quickly. He was lying in bed and he slowly came to the door. This one lost patience, this soldier and he shot through the door. And when he opened the door, he saw the man was bleeding. The neighbours who were there started shouting at him, "But he is a Serb, you wounded our man," and he panicked and he ran away. And I realised that this mistake of his saved my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Did you ever meet President Kovacevic after the takeover of power in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. What happened was that at the end of July or the beginning of August when we heard that international observers and reporters and the Red Cross had discovered the camps in Prijedor and the International Community had brought some stronger pressure to bear in connection with those camps, the intensity of arrests decreased and I felt freer and one day I went to my own apartment. I think this was early in August, somewhere there. However, on that day, some time in the afternoon, the police came and knocked on my door and they simply said that they were looking for me. At first, I thought they were maybe looking for someone else who had the same name, but he said, no, that they were looking for me. That some people from the International Community, some reporters had come and they wanted to see me in the halls of the Ljubija Mine, the dining room, the so-called red hall. I had no choice but to go with them. So these two policemen took me there. When I entered this hall in the mines, I saw inside Kovacevic, the chief of police Drljaca, one of the directors of the mines, a lawyer from the mines, another police officer and a journalist of Newsday, Roy Gutman, and he was the one who was looking for me. He had a list and he wanted to see whether I was alive. As soon as I entered, Kovacevic told me, sort of quietly, under his breath, "These men are asking for you. I thought that you were dead or in Omarska." So I saw that he was surprised to see me there. I sat there for a while. This Roy Gutman had some questions for me and then they took me back home. I remember that I asked the chief of police on that occasion, as Roy Gutman asked me, what it was that I wanted to do, what my intentions were in Prijedor. I said that I wanted to leave the town, that simply there was no life for me there any longer. And I asked the chief of police whether he knew of any safe convoys leaving Prijedor. And he said openly, "The only safe convoy are those escorted by the International Community. These others are not." And I had earlier heard this, but this actually confirmed what I had heard, that many convoys heading towards Travnik from Prijedor, that the buses came back bloodied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Was Drljaca the chief of police at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Was he responsible for some of the convoys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I do know from people who had heard how the convoys were organised, that the convoy was escorted by the police. So I assumed he should have been responsible. How the coordination actually worked, I really don't know. But according to the plan, convoys should have been provide with security. But he openly said of those convoys, that they were not safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: So it was your impression that neither the convoys organised by the Red Cross nor convoys with police security were safe for you and your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: And do you know who was the leader of Prijedor Red Cross at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: According to what I was able to learn, because all the information I obtained was from second- or third-hand, that it was the former President of the SDS Srdjo Srdic. [In English] It is wrong on the screen -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to show the witness and introduce document number 115 in the Prosecution Rule 65 ter exhibit list. The original has ERN number 00634034. It is one page. The English translation has number -- ERN number 03006814 at the top of the page.

utterances.text: Please read the document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbian municipality of Prijedor, Executive Board, number 02-111-64/92, date: 4th of May, 1992. utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Mrs. Sabiha Obradovic, as far as I know, is a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have two extra copies here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: MR. BERGSMO
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honour, only one extra copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would be provisional S23.

utterances.text: May I ask the witness to read the document, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbian municipality of Prijedor, Executive Board, number 02-111-58/92, date: 4th of May, 1992.
